content: Negotiators at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, released a revised draft agreement on Thursday that drops every reference to fossil fuels, the main driver of global warming, just one day before the talks are due to end. The new text, unveiled by co-host Australia, makes no mention of coal, oil or gas by name, and removes an earlier proposal for accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, according to [UN News](https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/11/1168839). The nearly 200 countries at the summit now have until Friday to agree a final deal, although climate negotiations have frequently run past their deadlines in the past. The draft, known as the cover decision, is meant to capture the outcome of COP31 and set the direction of climate action for the years ahead. Its silence on fossil fuels is striking because it comes two years after countries agreed at COP28 in Dubai to transition away from fossil fuels, and one year after the COP30 summit in Brazil ended with no mention of them in its final agreement either. Many governments had arrived in Antalya pressing for stronger language this time, and the removal has angered environmental groups and activists. Outside the venue on Thursday morning, campaigners held up crumpled missing-cat posters for a cat named Ambition, a stunt first staged at COP29 that has become a symbol of fading climate ambition. The Philippine campaigner Menager of the Ecología y Desarrollo Foundation told reporters that Ambition had apparently been disappearing ever since. The draft is roughly half the length of the earlier 18-page text, which had laid out competing national positions on energy, finance and trade. Oil-producing nations and fossil fuel lobbyists are reported to have pushed back hard against the phase-out language, and Australia's Climate Change Minister Chris Bowen, who is steering the negotiations, defended the slimmer text as the price of reaching an agreement all countries could support. He told a press conference in Antalya that the commitment made at COP28 to transition away from fossil fuels still stands, and that the aim was a deal every delegation could sign. UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell backed him, insisting that the COP28 commitment could not simply be erased. The commitment to transition away from fossil fuels was made in COP28, he said, and that commitment is very clear. What the draft does keep is significant in its own way. For the first time, a climate summit text acknowledges that the world will fail to hold warming to the 1.5 degrees Celsius limit set out in the Paris Agreement. The draft expresses deep concern that warming is projected to exceed that threshold, and recognises that every additional increment of warming above current levels will increase the frequency and intensity of heatwaves, floods and other extremes. It also reaffirms the goal of tripling adaptation finance for developing countries by 2035, although it leaves the details of how that increase is calculated for further discussion. And it puts electrification at the centre of the energy transition, calling for electricity to supply 35 percent of global final energy demand by 2035, a target championed by summit host Türkiye and known as 35 by 35. The text strongly reaffirms multilateralism and states that the global transition towards low greenhouse gas emissions and climate-resilient development is irreversible. The draft is the product of days of tense consultations. On Wednesday evening, COP31 President Murat Kurum gathered ministers for a Divan, a Turkish-style political exchange inspired by Ottoman tradition, in an effort to break the deadlock. Finance, adaptation and just transition talks remain unresolved as the Friday deadline approaches, and negotiators were expected to continue consultations into Thursday night. The summit is unfolding against a difficult global backdrop, with a record-breaking El Niño, climate-related disasters stretching from Europe to Nepal, and a global energy shock triggered by the war in Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and pushed oil prices higher, as covered in [our report on the tanker attacks](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/us-destroys-five-iranian-tankers-iran-retaliates-jordan-november-2026). For vulnerable nations, the stakes are concrete. Small island states and least developed countries have pushed hardest for both strong fossil fuel language and firm adaptation finance, arguing that they face the worst consequences of warming they did least to cause. The draft's promise to triple adaptation funding by 2035 matters to them, but without agreed numbers and a timetable it remains a pledge rather than a plan. The UN Climate Change Yearbook released at the summit found improvement in only 44 of 96 global climate indicators, a reminder of how far implementation lags behind promises. The coming hours will decide whether COP31 ends with a consensus all countries can accept or with another summit that sidesteps the hardest question. If ministers cannot bridge the divide over fossil fuels, the talks could spill into the weekend, as they have at previous summits. Even then, the question will not go away: a climate agreement that does not name the main cause of global warming leaves the central task of the energy transition to be fought again at the next summit. Campaigners have made the same point in blunter terms, warning that a deal which avoids naming coal, oil and gas risks being remembered as the summit where ambition went missing. The contrast with corporate accountability elsewhere was underlined this week when mining giant Rio Tinto agreed to pay 250 million dollars into a fund addressing the legacy of its Panguna copper mine in Papua New Guinea, as reported in [our coverage of the settlement](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/rio-tinto-250-million-panguna-mine-legacy-fund-november-2026). For now, the draft stands as a compromise that pleases almost no one fully: it concedes the 1.5 degree overshoot, keeps the electrification and adaptation goals alive, and drops the language that would have committed countries to ending fossil fuel use. Whether that trade-off holds through Friday's final plenary will determine whether COP31 is judged a pragmatic success or a retreat.
summary: A revised COP31 draft agreement released in Antalya on Thursday drops all references to fossil fuels, acknowledging for the first time that the world will overshoot the 1.5°C limit, as nearly 200 countries race to reach a final deal by Friday.
title: COP31 draft drops fossil fuel phase-out as summit nears Friday deadline
